kingdom.summary: Green leaves and stems that grow in one place and make food from sunlight point to the plant kingdom. Fungi lack chlorophyll and absorb their food, Chromista are mostly brown seaweeds and microscopic golden algae, and protozoa are mostly single-celled. Plants share chlorophylls a and b, starch for storage and cellulose cell walls.

options.47126: Multicellular organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis using chlorophylls a and b, store starch, and have cellulose cell walls. Most are green and grow anchored in one place.
options.47170: Absorb food from their surroundings instead of photosynthesising, and have chitin in their cell walls. Seen as mushrooms, brackets, moulds or (with algal partners) lichens, never as green leafy shoots.
options.48222: Mostly aquatic: kelps and other brown seaweeds, diatoms and their relatives. Photosynthetic members use chlorophyll c plus brownish pigments such as fucoxanthin, giving golden-brown to olive colours.
options.47686: Mostly single-celled organisms such as amoebae and slime moulds that usually feed on other organisms. They never form leafy, rooted, photosynthetic bodies.

phylum.summary: This plant has true roots, upright stems and leaves with veins, which come from vascular tissue (xylem and phloem). Algae, mosses, liverworts and hornworts lack that plumbing, so they stay small, flat or live in water. Veined leaves and sturdy stems are the easiest giveaway.

options.211194: Vascular plants: they have xylem and phloem, tissues that carry water and food, so they can grow tall with true roots, stems and veined leaves. Includes lycophytes, ferns, conifers and flowering plants.
options.50863: Green algae, living mostly in water, from single cells to sheets like sea lettuce. They share plant pigments but have no roots, vascular tissue or embryos nourished by a parent plant.
options.57774: Red algae: mostly marine seaweeds coloured red to purple by phycoerythrin pigment. No vascular tissue, true roots or leaves, and no swimming (flagellated) cells.
options.311249: Mosses: small leafy shoots anchored by thread-like rhizoids, without true roots or xylem and phloem. The green leafy plant is the long-lived stage; spores come from a capsule on a stalk.

class.summary: Flowers and fruits mark this as a flowering plant, which rules out the spore-bearing lycophytes and ferns and the cone-bearing conifers. Broad leaves with a branching network of veins, and flower parts in fours or fives, point to the dicots rather than the monocots, whose leaves usually have parallel veins and whose flower parts come in threes.

options.47623: Lycophytes (clubmosses, spikemosses, quillworts): spore-bearing vascular plants with small single-veined leaves, often with spores in cone-like tips. No flowers or seeds.
options.121943: Ferns (and horsetails): spore-bearing vascular plants without flowers or seeds. Fern fronds uncoil from fiddleheads and carry spore clusters on their undersides.
options.47124: Dicots: flowering plants usually with net-veined leaves, flower parts in fours or fives, and two seed leaves. Includes most broad-leaved trees, shrubs and wildflowers.
options.136329: Conifers: seed plants with needle- or scale-like leaves and seeds carried on cone scales rather than inside a fruit. No flowers.

order.summary: The flowers here are pea-like: a large upper petal (banner), two side petals (wings) and two lower petals joined into a keel, and the fruit is a pod. That combination marks Fabales. The other orders shown have radially symmetric flowers, daisy-like heads or fused bell-shaped petals instead.

options.47132: Roses, elms, figs and relatives: radially symmetric flowers with five free petals and many stamens on a cup-like rim, or tiny wind-pollinated flowers.
options.71289: Saxifrages, stonecrops, currants and relatives: mostly herbs or succulents with separate, radially symmetric petals and an ovary often with diverging beaks.
options.47181: Heaths, primroses, balsams and relatives: petals often fused into a bell, urn or tube, and stamens often attached to the petals.
options.47123: Pea-flowered plants and milkworts: flowers usually pea-like (a large upper banner, two side wings, a keel) or with two big petal-like sepals; fruits often pods; leaves often compound.

family.summary: The legume family is the one with true pea flowers (banner, wings and keel), compound leaves with stipules and pod fruits. Milkworts only mimic a pea flower, using two petal-like sepals as wings. The soapbark and bay-cedar families are small groups of trees and shrubs from elsewhere with simple leaves and no pea flowers.

options.71608: Soapbark family: a single genus of evergreen trees from Chile and nearby, with simple leaves, star-shaped flowers and star-shaped dry fruits.
options.61207: Milkwort family: small flowers that look pea-like but are built differently, with two large coloured petal-like sepals (wings) and a lower petal often fringed.
options.71636: Bay-cedar family: a small, mostly tropical and Australian group of shrubs and trees with simple leaves; none in BC.
options.47122: Legume family: pea-shaped flowers with banner, wings and keel; fruit a pod (legume); leaves usually compound with stipules; roots often with nitrogen-fixing nodules.

genus.summary: Trifolium has three leaflets joined at a single point and small flowers crowded into round heads, the old petals staying on. Medicks also have three leaflets, but the middle one sits on its own short stalk and the pods are often coiled. Lupines have hand-like leaves with five or more leaflets and tall spikes; sweet peas have tendrils.

options.51876: Clovers: three leaflets joined at one point; flowers in dense round heads, the petals withering in place around the small pod.
options.50321: Sweet peas and vetchlings: pinnate leaves with few leaflets ending in tendrils; stems often winged; fairly large flowers in loose racemes.
options.47121: Lupines: palmate leaves with five to many leaflets radiating like fingers; tall spikes of pea flowers, often blue or purple; hairy pods.
options.53152: Medicks (including alfalfa): three toothed leaflets, the middle one on a short stalk; small heads or racemes; pods usually coiled or curved, sometimes spiny.

species.summary: Tomcat clover is a native annual of dry grassy slopes and meadows in southwest BC, with narrow linear leaflets and purple, white-tipped flowers sitting in a conspicuous saucer of toothed bracts (involucre). Springbank clover has a similar involucre but is a creeping perennial of wet places with broader leaflets. White clover creeps and has white heads with no involucre; large hop clover has yellow heads.

options.57081: Tomcat clover: hairless annual from a taproot; leaflets linear to narrowly oblong, 1 to 4 cm; purple flowers, often white-tipped, above a shallowly lobed, toothed involucre; dry meadows and rock outcrops.
options.71146: Springbank clover: perennial spreading by rhizomes in moist meadows, streambanks and coastal sites; broader, toothed leaflets; red-purple flowers above a deeply cut involucre.
options.55745: White clover: introduced, creeping by rooting stolons; white or pinkish heads on long stalks without an involucre; leaflets broad, often with a pale V-band.
options.79409: Large hop clover: introduced annual or biennial with bright yellow heads that age to brown, like small hops; terminal leaflet unstalked.
